title: Explicit continuous unit-pivot Schur elimination
statement: Let $A$ be a commutative topological ring, let $T$ be a topological space, let $m,n\geq1$, and let $K:T\to\operatorname{Mat}_{n\times m}(A)$ [def-weil-matrix] have entrywise continuous entries. Suppose $a(t)=K_{11}(t)$ is a unit for every $t$ and $t\mapsto a(t)^{-1}$ is continuous. Define $L_0(t)$ to be diagonal with $a(t)^{-1}$ in the $(1,1)$ position and $1$ elsewhere, define $R_0(t)$ to be the identity with $(1,j)$ entry $-a(t)^{-1}K_{1j}(t)$ for $j>1$, and define $L_1(t)$ to be the identity with $(i,1)$ entry $-a(t)^{-1}K_{i1}(t)$ for $i>1$. Put $L(t)=L_0(t)L_1(t)$ and $H_{ij}(t)=K_{ij}(t)-a(t)^{-1}K_{i1}(t)K_{1j}(t)$ for $i,j$ in the reduced index sets. Then $L$ and $R_0$ are entrywise continuous maps to $\operatorname{GL}_n(A)$ and $\operatorname{GL}_m(A)$ with entrywise continuous inverses, $H$ has continuous entries, and $L(t)K(t)R_0(t)=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&H(t)\end{pmatrix}$ for every $t$.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 6.12(2), finite E case, pp. 18–19: continuous integral division and elementary pivot elimination; the displayed auxiliary statement is written out here because HRS uses it as a standard calculation.

proof.text: Write $b(t)=a(t)^{-1}$, so $a(t)b(t)=b(t)a(t)=1$. Matrices are entry families as in [def-weil-matrix]; multiplication here is the finite sum $(XY)_{ij}=\sum_k X_{ik}Y_{kj}$. Set $N=L_1-I_n$ and $P=R_0-I_m$. Only the entries $N_{i1}=-bK_{i1}$ for $i>1$ can be nonzero, and row $1$ of $N$ is zero, so every summand $N_{ik}N_{kj}$ vanishes. Thus $N^2=0$. Likewise only $P_{1j}=-bK_{1j}$ for $j>1$ can be nonzero, and column $1$ of $P$ is zero, so $P^2=0$. Expanding gives $(I+N)(I-N)=(I-N)(I+N)=I$ and the same identities for $P$. Hence $L_1^{-1}=I-N$ and $R_0^{-1}=I-P$.

source.place: Agent auxiliary calculation for the continuous-pivot step; HRS Theorem 6.12(2), printed pp. 18–19, motivates continuous division but does not state this matrix identity.

proof.text: The diagonal matrix $D=\operatorname{diag}(a,1,\ldots,1)$ satisfies $DL_0=L_0D=I_n$, using $ab=ba=1$. Therefore the prescribed product $L=L_0L_1$ has two-sided inverse $(I-N)D$: multiplication in either order cancels adjacent inverse factors. Entrywise, $L_{11}=b$, $L_{i1}=-bK_{i1}$ for $i>1$, and all remaining entries are those of $I_n$. Its inverse has $(L^{-1})_{11}=a$, $(L^{-1})_{i1}=K_{i1}$ for $i>1$, and the remaining identity entries, since $bK_{i1}a=K_{i1}$ by commutativity. Thus $L(t)\in\operatorname{GL}_n(A)$ and $R_0(t)\in\operatorname{GL}_m(A)$ for every $t$; here $\operatorname{GL}_r(A)$ means the square matrices with a two-sided multiplicative inverse.

source.place: Agent auxiliary calculation for the continuous-pivot step; HRS Theorem 6.12(2), printed pp. 18–19, motivates continuous division but does not state this matrix identity.

proof.text: Fix $t$ and suppress it in the notation. Column $1$ of $R_0$ is the first basis column, so $(KR_0)_{i1}=K_{i1}$. For $j>1$ its column $j$ has only the diagonal entry $1$ and the extra entry $-bK_{1j}$ in row $1$. Thus $(KR_0)_{ij}=K_{ij}-K_{i1}bK_{1j}$. In particular $(KR_0)_{1j}=K_{1j}-abK_{1j}=0$ for $j>1$, and $(KR_0)_{11}=a$. For $i,j>1$ the same formula is precisely $H_{ij}$, because $A$ is commutative.

source.place: Agent auxiliary calculation for the continuous-pivot step; HRS Theorem 6.12(2), printed pp. 18–19, motivates continuous division but does not state this matrix identity.

proof.text: Put $B=KR_0$. Row $1$ of $L_1$ is the first basis row, and for $i>1$, $(L_1B)_{ij}=B_{ij}-bK_{i1}B_{1j}$. At $j=1$ this is $K_{i1}-bK_{i1}a=0$. At $j>1$, $B_{1j}=0$, so it is $H_{ij}$. Consequently $L_1KR_0$ has corner $a$, zero remaining entries in its first row and column, and reduced block $H$. Left multiplication by $L_0$ multiplies only row $1$ by $b$, changing that corner to $ba=1$. This proves $LKR_0=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&H\end{pmatrix}$ with exactly the order $L_0L_1$ in the statement.

source.place: Agent auxiliary calculation for the continuous-pivot step; HRS Theorem 6.12(2), printed pp. 18–19, motivates continuous division but does not state this matrix identity.

proof.text: For each fixed entry index, the displayed entries of $L$, $L^{-1}$, $R_0$ and $R_0^{-1}$ are constants or one of $a$, $b$, $K_{i1}$, $\pm bK_{i1}$, $\pm bK_{1j}$. The functions $a$ and all $K_{ij}$ are continuous by hypothesis, and $b$ is continuous by the separate hypothesis on the pivot inverse. Products, negatives and differences of these functions are continuous: for example $t\mapsto(b(t),K_{i1}(t))$ is continuous into $A\times A$, and composing with the continuous ring multiplication gives $bK_{i1}$; negation and subtraction work in the same way. Applying this twice to $H_{ij}=K_{ij}-bK_{i1}K_{1j}$ proves continuity of every residual entry. These are exactly the entrywise continuity assertions, including those of both inverse families; no continuity of inversion on the whole unit group is needed.

source.place: Agent auxiliary calculation for the continuous-pivot step; HRS Theorem 6.12(2), printed pp. 18–19, motivates continuous division but does not state this matrix identity.

proof.text: When $n=1$ there are no indices $i>1$, and when $m=1$ there are no indices $j>1$. The corresponding reduced block has an empty row or column set; the same finite-sum calculations still apply. In particular for $m=n=1$ they give $b\,a=1$. If $T$ is empty all pointwise assertions are vacuous and the unique entry functions are continuous. Thus the calculation covers every case allowed by $m,n\geq1$.

reviewed.note: mechanical checks by tools/merge_delivery.py; mathematics reviewed in full by NT-cc-Q23-06a1e72a8 (reviewer sub-agent of L); spot-checked: I read the whole item: the statement and all 6 steps. I also read def-weil-matrix, which supplies only the entry-family notion the item uses, and the consumer lem-sfb-continuous-integral-pivot-splitting, whose step 1 applies the item with the same order L0L1, R0 and residual block. I recomputed every step by hand. Step 1: N^2=0 and P^2=0, so the inverses are I-N and I-P. Step 2: L^{-1}=(I-N)D, with entries a and K_i1. Step 3: column elimination makes row 1 vanish because ab=1. Step 4: row elimination uses ba=1; L0 then scales row 1 by b to give a corner of 1, and the order is correct by associativity. Step 5: continuity uses only the topological-ring operations and the separate hypothesis that the pivot inverse is continuous. Step 6: empty blocks and empty T. Every step is honestly elementary. I ran my own test on 16200 random cases over Z/1, Z/4, Z/6, Z/8, Z/9 and Z/12 with shapes up to 3x3; all identities and both two-sided inverses hold. The delivery has no new nodes, so no duplicate, restated-clause or drop question arises. The proof cites no statement node, so it stays on its route, has no tool_uses and cites no SGA. lean.statement: theorem continuous_unitPivot_schur_formula {A : Type u} [CommRing A] [TopologicalSpace A] [IsTopologicalRing A] {T : Type v} [TopologicalSpace T] {n m : ℕ} (K : T → Matrix (Fin (n + 1)) (Fin (m + 1)) A) (hK : ∀ i j, Continuous (fun t => K t i j)) (hunit : ∀ t, IsUnit (K t 0 0)) (hinv : Continuous (fun t => Ring.inverse (K t 0 0))) : (∀ t, IsUnit (unitPivotLeft (K t))) ∧ (∀ t, IsUnit (unitPivotRightElimination (K t))) ∧ (∀ i j, Continuous (fun t => unitPivotLeft (K t) i j)) ∧ (∀ i j, Continuous (fun t => unitPivotRightElimination (K t) i j)) ∧ (∀ i j, Continuous (fun t => Ring.inverse (unitPivotLeft (K t)) i j)) ∧ (∀ i j, Continuous (fun t => Ring.inverse (unitPivotRightElimination (K t)) i j)) ∧ (∀ i j, Continuous (fun t => unitPivotSchurComplement (K t) i j)) ∧ (∀ t, unitPivotLeft (K t) * K t * unitPivotRightElimination (K t) = of (Fin.cases (Fin.cases 1 (fun _ => 0)) (fun i => Fin.cases 0 (unitPivotSchurComplement (K t) i))))
lean.note: Positive dimensions are n + 1 and m + 1. The five helper definitions are the prescribed factors and residual block of this node. IsUnit expresses membership in the general linear group, and Ring.inverse agrees with the inverse of each unit.

reviewed_lean.note: The Lean statement matches every hypothesis and conclusion of the node: arbitrary commutative topological ring, independent universes u and v, sizes n+1 and m+1, entrywise-continuous K, unit pivot with continuous Ring.inverse, L0, L1 and R0 as prescribed, L=L0*L1, H on the successor indices. The eight conjuncts give IsUnit, entry continuity of the matrices and their inverses, continuity of H, and L*K*R0 = diag(1,H) with the Fin.cases layout checked.
